meta.audience: Each commander writing to the other
principles: A negotiation opened by the losing side
Two accounts of the same history
Terms that cost the other side more than they gain

world_behind.title: Ammoron opens the negotiation
world_behind.text: Verse 1 has him send to Moroni asking for an exchange. The side holding Nephite civilians is the one that wants to trade.

world_behind.title: Moroni has a supply reason and a manpower reason
world_behind.text: Verse 2 says he wanted the provisions spent on Lamanite prisoners and wanted his own people back in his army.

world_behind.title: The prisoner populations are not alike
world_behind.text: Verse 3 says the Lamanites hold women and children and Moroni holds none. That asymmetry produces the terms in verse 11, and Alma 55:16 and 17 shows what it cost: Nephite women and children behind a wall, armed in silence to get themselves out.

world_behind.title: Moroni calls it a stratagem
world_behind.text: Verse 3 calls his own letter a stratagem. The word appears seven times in the volume and every one of them falls inside this war: Alma 43:30, 52:10, 54:3, 56:30, 58:6, 58:28 and 62:35. It is the vocabulary of a single campaign and of no other.

world_behind.title: Ammoron gives a rival version of Nephite history
world_behind.text: Verses 17 and 18 say the fathers wronged their brethren and robbed them of the government. Mosiah 10:12 to 17 gives the same grievance in full, as the tradition Lamanite children are taught, four hundred years of standing complaint compressed into one sentence of a war letter.

world_behind.title: He names his own descent
world_behind.text: Verse 23 says he is a descendant of Zoram, which makes the man leading the Lamanites a Nephite by ancestry twice over.

world_behind.title: Both letters are given whole
world_behind.text: Mormon quotes ten verses of Moroni and nine of Ammoron without summarizing either. The chapter is almost entirely other people's words.

words.text: A formal letter. The word occurs forty-one times in this record and fourteen in the King James Bible, and most of the record's uses are in Alma 54 through 62. Mormon uses the exchange of letters as the main vehicle of this part of the war.

The place of the damned. The phrase child of hell occurs twice in this record and once in the King James Bible, where Christ uses it of a proselyte made worse by his teachers. Moroni applies it to Ammoron before naming his terms.

To exact retribution. It appears eight times in the record, and the King James Bible seventeen. Ammoron uses it twice, of his brother's blood and of his people's wrongs, and it is the stated ground of his whole war.
Treated at Alma 35:9, of the Zoramite ruler. Ammoron turns the word back on Moroni in the same sentence that says he does not fear them, which is the letter's one moment of direct reply.
Being wiped out entirely. The word occurs once in scripture. Ammoron names it as one of two acceptable ends to a war he calls eternal, the other being Nephite submission.
Compelled, forced along. The record uses it twice and the King James Bible fifteen times. Ammoron says the Nephite fathers pressed Zoram out of Jerusalem, which is his reading of 1 Nephi 4.

phrases.term: Moroni felt to rejoice exceedingly at this request
phrases.text: Mormon reports the reaction before the letter. The request is good news because of provisions and manpower, which sets the negotiation in a frame the letter itself never mentions.

phrases.term: There was not a woman nor a child among all the prisoners of Moroni
phrases.text: The asymmetry stated plainly. It is the reason for the terms, and Mormon gives it before quoting a letter that never explains itself.
The record's own word for what follows. Alma 43 introduced the term for battlefield maneuver, and here it covers a letter.

phrases.term: This war which ye have waged against my people, or rather which thy brother hath waged
phrases.text: Moroni corrects himself mid-sentence to fix the responsibility. He is careful about who started it even while accusing the man who continued it.

phrases.term: It supposeth me that thou art a child of hell
phrases.text: The insult sits immediately before the terms. Moroni tells Ammoron the argument is wasted on him and then makes a concrete offer in the same verse.

phrases.term: Ye will deliver up a man and his wife and his children, for one prisoner
phrases.text: The terms. Four for one, and Mormon has already explained why: Moroni holds only soldiers, so any exchange returns families for fighting men.

phrases.term: I will arm my women and my children
phrases.text: The threat Moroni makes if the terms are refused. It is the most extreme thing he says, and verse 13 immediately returns to the claim that the Nephites have only sought to defend themselves.

phrases.term: I am Moroni; I am a leader of the people of the Nephites
phrases.text: The signature. He names himself and his office in seven words, and Ammoron opens his reply with a matching formula in verse 16.

phrases.term: Your fathers did wrong their brethren... and rob them of their right to the government
phrases.text: Ammoron's account of the quarrel. It is the Lamanite reading of the succession after Lehi, and Mormon lets it stand in the record without answering it.

phrases.term: If it so be that there is such a being, we know not but that he hath made us as well as you
phrases.text: Ammoron's answer to the theology. He grants nothing and concedes the possibility in the same sentence, then says these things matter not.

phrases.term: I am Ammoron, and a descendant of Zoram
phrases.text: The claim under his whole case. The man leading the Lamanites is of Nephite descent, and he names an ancestor whose treatment he calls compulsion.

verses.label: v. 5–7
verses.title: A refusal to speak, used three times to speak
verses.text: The letter says what it will not say: "I would tell you somewhat concerning the justice of God," then "I would tell you these things if ye were capable of hearkening unto them," then "I would tell you concerning that awful hell." Three conditional openings in two verses, each delivering the content it claims to withhold. The record preserves the device intact by giving the letter whole instead of summarizing its argument, so the reader gets the doctrine and the insult in the same clause.

verses.label: v. 14–16
verses.title: Two letters, three signatures, one convention
verses.text: The record preserves the sign-off of each writer, and they match in form: "I am Moroni; I am a leader of the people of the Nephites," and "I am Ammoron, the king of the Lamanites; I am the brother of Amalickiah." Ammoron then signs a second time at verse 23, "I am Ammoron, and a descendant of Zoram." Name, then office or lineage, in every case. Moroni claims a function and Ammoron claims a title and a bloodline, and the record lets the difference stand without comment.

chapter.title: The chapter is two letters and a frame
chapter.text: Nineteen of twenty-four verses are quoted correspondence. Mormon supplies the motive in verses 2 and 3 and then gets out of the way.

chapter.title: Mormon explains the terms before the letter states them
chapter.text: The reader knows about the prisoner asymmetry in verse 3, so verse 11 reads as a calculation rather than as cruelty.

chapter.title: Both men give a history of the war
chapter.text: Moroni traces it to Amalickiah; Ammoron traces it to a stolen government six centuries back. The record prints both accounts without arbitrating.

chapter.title: The insult and the offer share a verse
chapter.text: Moroni calls him a child of hell and proposes terms in the same breath. The letter is not trying to persuade and is trying to trade.

chapter.title: Ammoron's theology is agnostic rather than atheist
chapter.text: God is unknown to his people, unknown to Moroni as well, and if real then the maker of both peoples. Then he says it does not matter.

chapter.title: The Lamanite king is Nephite by descent
chapter.text: Amalickiah was a Nephite dissenter, and Ammoron claims descent from Zoram. Mormon has said since Alma 43 that dissenters run this war.

chapter.title: Both accept a deal neither wanted from the other
chapter.text: Ammoron proposed it, Moroni set hard terms, and Ammoron takes them for his own supply reasons. Alma 55 opens with Moroni refusing to honor it.

chapter.title: Each signs with an identity claim
chapter.text: Three signatures stand in the chapter and all three follow one form, name then standing. Verse 14: "I am Moroni; I am a leader of the people of the Nephites." Verse 16: "I am Ammoron, the king of the Lamanites; I am the brother of Amalickiah." Verse 23: "I am Ammoron, and a descendant of Zoram, whom your fathers pressed and brought out of Jerusalem." One man claims a function, the other a title and two lineages, and the second lineage is the grievance verses 17 and 18 are arguing.

applications.title: Know why you want the deal
applications.text: Moroni had two concrete reasons before he wrote a word. Before entering a negotiation, write down what you are actually trying to get.

applications.title: Look at what each side is holding
applications.text: The exchange terms followed from the prisoner asymmetry. When something is being traded, work out what each party has and what it costs them to part with it.

applications.title: Do not expect the letter to persuade
applications.text: Moroni said outright he thought the argument wasted. When you are dealing with someone who will not be moved by reasons, make the offer clear and stop trying.

applications.title: Say that you are angry instead of hiding it
applications.text: Moroni put "Behold, I am in my anger" into the letter in his own words. Naming your state in a hard exchange is more honest than letting it leak through the wording while you present yourself as calm.

applications.title: Read the other side's account of the history
applications.text: Ammoron had a story in which he was the wronged party. Understanding what your opponent believes happened is not the same as agreeing with it.

applications.title: Read the reason attached to the yes
applications.text: Ammoron granted the exchange so that he could preserve his food for his men of war, and he wrote the reason down. When someone agrees to something, the motive they give tells you how long the agreement will hold.

applications.title: Watch for the shrug that closes the subject
applications.text: Ammoron raised the devil and hell himself and then wrote "these things matter not". Someone who will not let a question count against him has stopped arguing with you and started handling you.

applications.title: Notice which ancestry gets claimed
applications.text: Ammoron traced himself to Zoram and then called himself a bold Lamanite. People select the lineage that licenses what they already mean to do, so listen for which one gets named and at what point in the argument.

questions.text: When something difficult arrives, do I know what I want out of it?
Whom do I hold responsible for a situation, and is that accurate?
Have I insulted someone in the same breath as asking them for something?
What is the most extreme thing I have threatened, and did I mean it?
What grievance from long ago still shapes how I act?
What do I say does not matter that I keep returning to?
What do I claim about my own descent or origin, and why does it matter to me?
